content:
This is a key observation in https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/08/18/palomar-a-registry-of-lean-verified-mathematics/ — “check… that the formal statements also match (in a semantic sense) the informal description of the claimed results”

How does Palomar plan to tackle this? The ML practitioner in me might suggest an initial benchmark dataset based on “translation” between informal and formal statements to measure accuracy of this task (for a given language model and prompt), however, this statistical approach doesn’t seem bulletproof in they way we may require.

Maybe we can use multiple models and measure the inter annotator agreement, e.g., so that we only admit a faithful translation if there is total agreement. This would not eliminate false positives but could help with robustness.

Open to thoughts here!

@Alex Korbonits, so far we just trust Sol to get it right. :woman_shrugging:

I would love to have someone do some research here, and propose alternative practical mechanisms (at no greater cost).

The palomar database gives anyone interested in doing this a great initial problem set to look at!

@Kim Morrison this is close to something I'm already working on! I have a paper in progress that would build a taxonomy of statement-level autoformalization errors from a hand-labeled corpus and evaluatesLLM judges against those labels per error class, rather than as a single pass/fail.

I intend to benchmark current models on exactly this problem using, e.g., Palomar's 02-statement-alignment.md as a baseline prompt, and compare it against a taxonomy-guided version on the same models. I'll share results here once they're in! Deadline for a workshop I'm thinking of submitting to is end of September.

One more suggestion would be to have other frontier models validate Sol’s review more like ensemble —for example Claude Opus/Fable, or even cheaper models—and have a controller compare the outputs. This can never replace a human mathematician, but it should still be more robust than trusting Sol alone.

It seems cheap in implementation effort, if not in dollars :slight_smile:—so Lean FRO would need to shell out a bit more. Given the nice Challenge template Palomar has defined, frontier models can already produce a good informal description of the claimed result quite easily (I have tried with existing results); checking that it is genuinely faithful is the harder part, in the end we trust @Kim Morrison :)
